title: Visiting graves
hookLine: visit graves, for they remind of the hereafter (Muslim)
last: THE EYES WEEP, THE TONGUE STAYS KIND.

cards: For a while, it was forbidden. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, had at first told his followers not to visit graves.
Then, in a hadith in Sahih Muslim, he reverses it, in Buraydah's report, in paraphrase: I had forbidden you to visit graves; now visit them.
A rule given, then lifted out loud, with the change left on the record for everyone to see. Why visiting the dead was opened up again, and what a graveyard is for.

teach.h: WHY FORBIDDEN? THE TEXT IS QUIET.
teach.b: The texts don't spell out why the first rule was given. Some readers suggest the early community was close to old customs of loud lament and worship at tombs, and needed distance from them first.
That's an explanation people offer, not something the hadith says. What the hadith does give is the reason for the opening.

In another report in Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, the Prophet visited the grave of his own mother. He wept there, and the people around him wept. And he said, in paraphrase: visit graves, for they remind you of death.
Some other collections carry the wording: they remind you of the hereafter. Either way, notice who the visit is for. Not mainly the dead.
The visitor. Each stone is a person who once had plans for next week. A name.
Flowers someone left. A path worn by other visitors.
And there's love in it too: a son, grown and leading a community, crying at his mother's grave.
He didn't treat the grave as a place to avoid. He went, he wept, and then he opened the door for everyone else to go. So a cemetery isn't only a place for the dead.
It's a classroom for the living, with very quiet teachers.

how: Muslims visit the graves of family and of the community, citing the hadith in Sahih Muslim where the Prophet lifted an earlier ban and said graves remind of death; visitors greet the dead, remember them and pray for them.

o: a practice the Prophet banned for good in Madinah
going to a cemetery to remember death and the hereafter
a yearly duty to tend the family tomb on a fixed date

p: I had forbidden you; now visit
the visit to his mother's grave

s: visiting graves was always allowed in Islam
the Prophet first forbade it, then said: now visit them.
the Prophet visited his own mother's grave and wept
Abu Hurayrah's report in Sahih Muslim says he wept, and those with him wept.
the hadith explains exactly why the first ban was given
the reason for the ban isn't spelled out; the reason for the opening is: they remind you.

games.q: you once told your community not to do something. now you see it would help them. what do you do?
o: quietly let people start doing it.
say plainly: I had forbidden it; now do it.
keep the old rule so you look consistent.
games.why: in Sahih Muslim the Prophet says it out loud: I had forbidden you to visit graves; now visit them.

practice: Think of a grave you know, a grandparent's, a friend's, a stranger's stone you once noticed on a walk, and stand there in your mind for a few breaths. Ask what it reminds you of, and what you'd want to say.
If you pray, you can remember the person who lies there.

wordCard.voice: Visiting graves. Once forbidden, then opened by the Prophet himself: go, because the graves remind you. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a visit, the word used for visiting graves.

carryVoice: Your line: they remind. Quiet teachers, every one of them. Go gently.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 977 (Buraydah: I had forbidden you to visit graves; now visit them)
Sahih Muslim 976 (Abu Hurayrah: the visit to his mother's grave; visit graves, for they remind of death)
Jami' al-Tirmidhi 1054 (variant: they remind of the hereafter)
